title: Constraining the Expressive Range of Shortest Paths
abstract: Expressive range metrics are often used to evaluate procedural level generators. Solution-path related metrics require using an agent that plays the level, often by finding a single shortest path through the level. However, there may be multiple shortest paths with different metrics. Additionally, in expressive range analysis, it is common to repeatedly generate levels for the agent to evaluate, which may be inefficient when a desired metric value is known. Recently, constraint-based approaches, which can solve for both a level and an example solution path, have been used to constrain metrics in generated levels. This example solution path, however, may not correspond to the one a shortest-path agent would take. We extend that work with path-state reachability, and the constraint that all shortest paths through a level have some desired expressive range metric value. We view agent-evaluated metrics as properties of paths through a reachability graph on locations in the level, and augment locations in the graph with path length and state-based information relevant to the metrics. We use this path-state reachability graph in the constraint problem to ensure that there is a path through the level with the desired metric value, and that any path with a different metric value is longer (or, in some cases, does not exist). We apply this to various path-based expressive range metrics in a top-down exploration game and platformer game, and compare to levels generated without path-state reachability. We find that the path-state reachability takes longer to generate levels, but may be more efficient for metric values that are less likely to be generated by chance.

title: JoMoHa: Joint Model--Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: The performance of language agents depends jointly on model weights and the harness. Optimizing either alone can be constrained by the other component, limiting overall performance gains. Our analysis of naive alternating training reveals progressive incompatibility between the model and harness, which increasingly interferes with task execution and may also undermine model training, leading to performance degradation. To coordinate the evolution of models and harnesses, we introduce JoMoHa, to our knowledge the first framework to jointly train an executable harness generation policy and a task execution policy through reinforcement learning. JoMoHa outperforms the evaluated weight-only and harness-only baselines and achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated methods on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, averaging 70.3% and reaching 97.0% on ALFWorld. By learning both task execution and runtime improvement from its own generated trajectories, JoMoHa performs recursive self-improvement (RSI).

title: A Layer-wise Study of How Style Rewriting Breaks the Calibration of Zero-Shot LLM Fake-News Detectors
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked to judge whether a news article is true, and their stated confidence is often taken at face value. We test what happens to that confidence when an article's writing style, but not its facts, is manipulated, as in recent \emph{style attacks} on fake-news detectors. Tracing how the prediction and its confidence form layer by layer inside the network, we study three model families (LLaMA-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B) on three fake-news benchmarks, and find the same three patterns in every model--dataset pairing. First, on the original articles the models are competent and largely honest judges: they settle on an answer, briefly become overconfident, and then correct their confidence in the final layers. Second, style-rewritten articles break this self-correction: the models become far less accurate, under the strongest attack, worse than random guessing, yet remain just as confident, so they are \emph{confidently wrong} precisely when a warning is most needed. Third, nearly all of the damage comes from rewriting into sensational or emotionally charged styles, while sober, neutral rewrites leave the models' honesty largely intact. The practical implication is that an LLM's confidence about veracity cannot be trusted as a safety signal when an article's style may have been manipulated.

title: A Hierarchical Planning Architecture to Play Time Management Games
abstract: Hierarchical task networks (HTNs) are used in games as drivers for efficiently-computed reactive and plausible NPC behaviors. In this paper, we propose a system that uses temporally-aware hierarchical semantics, which are central to time management games -resource management games where time is the primary resource to manage. Temporally-aware hierarchical reasoning problems are generally NEXP-complete in fully-grounded settings and 2-NEXP-complete in lifted settings. These problems are thus naively infeasible to solve in games contexts, which require either quick or clever ways for compute-intense tasks such that they avoid disrupting realtime gameplay. We present a novel plan-space planner for both the simple temporal case and temporally-uncertain execution case. We tested our planner on three domains: two modified from the 2020 hierarchical IPC competition and a novel domain based on our motivating game context, Overcooked. Our results suggest that extending HTNs with simple temporal information are feasible to solve in near real-time but that managing temporally uncertain execution remains infeasible to solve even with generous computational resource budgets. We discuss the relevance of these results toward our eventual goal of agents that can automatically play time management games as cooperative player partners and as gameplay testing agents.

title: Branch-and-Commit for Frozen RL Agents: When and Where to Spend Test-Time Compute
abstract: Reinforcement learning agents are often deployed with policies that cannot be retrained or modified. In digital environments whose states can be copied and resumed, an operator has another option: sample several continuations from the current state, evaluate them, and continue from the endpoint of the selected branch. We call this procedure branch-and-commit. We study when it improves return, what produces the improvement, and where its computational budget should be spent. Across four environments, two frozen policies, five continuation verifiers, and a model-free selection rule, we find that the benefit of branching depends on dispersion: the difference between the best candidate return and the mean candidate return. Branching provides no benefit in low-dispersion settings, while increasing return by 12.8% in our main Craftax-Medium setting. Most of this gain comes not from selecting better actions, but from selecting among different stochastic realizations of the same action. Several competent verifiers achieve similar episode returns, suggesting that verifier quality is not the main constraint at our operating budget. Instead, computation is better allocated to states where useful dispersion is likely. On held-out seeds, gating branching using predicted dispersion retains 69% of the improvement from uniform branching while using 48% as many branching calls. These results characterize when branch-and-commit is useful and clarify what its gains represent.

title: FRESCO: A Novel Consistency Control for Asynchronous Pipeline Parallel Training
abstract: Asynchronous pipeline parallelism can accelerate distributed model training, but suffers from instability caused by inconsistent gradient computations. We identify a fundamental source of this inconsistency: error signals are coupled to forward-time features, not just parameter states. This means that parameters may evolve as long as they preserve forward-equivalence. Leveraging this insight, we introduce FRESCO, which frames asynchronous updates as a constrained optimization problem: it finds the minimal update modification that acts trivially on the activation subspace. We demonstrate that FRESCO consistently outperforms representative asynchronous baselines in LLM pre-training, with the gains most pronounced under deep pipelines and high inconsistency levels: at pipeline depth 32, it reaches the same loss as the strongest baseline with 43% fewer iterations and 30% less wall-clock time, while requiring 8~921$\times$ less memory overhead. Moving beyond the current limitations, FRESCO establishes a new foundation for high-utilization pipeline parallel training, providing a scalable path for large-model development on diverse, resource-constrained systems.

title: TID System for Speech-COSER Challenge 2026: ASR Track
abstract: We describe the system submitted by Telefónica Innovación Digital to the Speech-COSER Challenge 2026, which features spontaneous speech from elderly speakers recorded in rural Spain. For ASR, we perform CTC-based pseudo-forced alignment scores audio-text match quality to guide a two-stage LoRA curriculum, followed by post-hoc magnitude pruning of the LoRA matrices to enhance generalization. An ensemble of seven systems combined via ROVER achieves 36.25\% unnormalized and 22.17\% normalized WER.

title: LoMASA: A Local Multi-Agent Sales Assistant with Confidence-Gated Delegation for B2B Quoting
abstract: Frontline sales staff spend much of their day re-coordinating quotes after customers change quantities, ask for discounts or new payment terms, or costs move. We present LoMASA (Local Multi-Agent Sales Assistant), a training-free multi-agent system that runs entirely on one desktop computer. A 35B mixture-of-experts model (System-1) makes each decision in a single forward pass and reads its confidence from the probabilities of the answer options. A 27B dense model (System-2) writes customer replies and escalation briefs and is consulted when System-1 is unsure. Code computes every price, margin and option, and hard pricing rules cannot be overridden. On a test split of 500 simulated episodes with 1512 decisions built from public supply-chain data, the salesperson has to decide only 19.5% of decisions: 38.0% are settled automatically, with a median latency of 2.67 seconds, and 42.5% are escalated to a manager by the hard rules. On the automatically settled decisions LoMASA is as accurate as a rule baseline (0.894 vs.\ 0.894) and makes fewer commitments whose margin later falls below the floor (2.61% vs 4.53%); the price is additional escalations to the manager. Option probabilities are well calibrated without any training, unlike confidence stated in words by the same model. We also report where the design does not help: the 27B model rarely changes a decision.

title: Regret without Optimal-Arm Feedback under Reward-Dependent Delays
abstract: We study stochastic bandits with reward-dependent delays, possibly infinite, whose reports omit the originating round. For each $c\in[0,1)$, Balanced Historical Optimism (BHO) has a delay term controlled by the largest suboptimal-arm quantile at level $1-cΔ_i$, without requiring optimal-arm reports. Lower bounds give an inverse-square slack cost in the logarithmic statistical regime and linear minimax regret at $c=1$. A family with growing $K$ forces worst-case regret $Ω(G\log K)$ for every learner, where $G=\max_iΔ_i h_i$ is the largest gap-weighted suboptimal cutoff. Pending-triggered balance preserves BHO's weighted-cutoff bound for $c<1$ and attains the historical-greedy exploration coefficient with deterministic rewards, a unique optimum and fixed bounded delays. Gap-weighted comparisons and experiments show when shared waiting helps and what balanced exploration costs.

title: SegDis: Foreground Segmentation Followed by Type Discrimination for Salient and Camouflaged Object Detection
abstract: Salient and camouflaged object detection (SOD and COD) both recover foreground support, yet most joint methods output only a binary mask and therefore cannot distinguish the type. USC12K distinguishes the two types, but its baseline USCNet still binds foreground existence to the type within a single normalization, so the failure source cannot be attributed. Our cross-task study shows that foreground localization transfers between SOD and COD, whereas type discrimination does not: a COD-only model recovers foreground on SOD images but its type judgement follows the training distribution rather than the foreground-background relation, so the two decisions require separate mechanisms. SegDis factorizes the output into an explicit foreground probability and a conditional type probability given foreground: FLR provides high-quality task-agnostic support, and RTA refines the SOD/COD assignment from the foreground-background relation without a task identifier. Because support is explicit, each ground-truth foreground pixel is classified as correct-type, type-swapped, or missed, so foreground-recovery and type-assignment errors are diagnosed separately. With PVT-v2-B2, SegDis attains 68.98% FG-mIoU and 78.35% mIoU on USC12K at about one-eighth of USCNet's parameters; CSCS is 5.75.

title: TLRS-DPO: Token-Level Risk Scoring for Better Direct Preference Optimization
abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a simple and widely used alternative to RLHF for aligning large language models (LLMs), but its sequence-level objective cannot precisely locate or suppress the local patterns that make an otherwise acceptable response unsafe or undesirable. We propose TLRS-DPO (Token-Level Risk Scoring for Better Direct Preference Optimization), which augments DPO with fine-grained token-level control while remaining fully offline and reference-based. TLRS-DPO introduces a token-level robust compensation term that converts the policy-reference log-ratio on rejected responses into localized risk scores, a curriculum-style schedule that gradually increases the strength of this compensation during training, and a risk-adaptive screening mechanism that selectively penalizes only high-risk tokens instead of entire sequences. This design bridges sequence-level preference fitting and token-level behavior control, and can be implemented as a drop-in modification to standard DPO trainers. Empirically, TLRS-DPO improves alignment quality and safety-relevant behavior with minimal impact on helpfulness compared to strong DPO baselines.

title: Learning through Capacity Awareness to Minimize Hospital Readmissions
abstract: Predictive algorithms are increasingly used to guide hospital discharge decisions, yet these models can exhibit censoring bias for vulnerable patients due to insufficient historical data or past discharge decisions. When biased readmission risk predictors are used to inform discharges, the training data generated by discharge decisions may perpetuate similar biases when predictors are re-trained, leading to a vicious cycle. We extend a queueing-based Markov decision process for hospital discharge to incorporate periodically retrained readmission risk predictors. Our key insight is that cost-optimal, "capacity-aware" operational decision policies can naturally diversify the lengths of stay at which patient outcomes are observed, enabling consistent estimation of readmission risk without explicit fairness constraints. We prove that repeated retraining under discharge-up-to policies converges to unbiased risk estimates under well-specification. In synthetic experiments and calibrated simulations based on patient-level data from a partner hospital, we find that where commonly used threshold-on-risk policies can remain persistently biased, discharge-up-to policies reduce learning error over status quo decision policies (such as thresholding on risk) by 24%-25%. These improvements to estimation also mitigate some forms of bias, reducing readmission cost disparities (adjusted for baseline risk differences between demographic groups) by 38%-63%. Our results demonstrate how capacity-aware decision policies can improve both predictive performance and fairness by addressing censoring bias.

title: MCSA: Multi-Cutoff Spectral Aggregation in SO(3) Equivariant GNNs for Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) based on Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (EGNNs) have achieved remarkable progress in atomistic modeling. However, accurately representing atomic interactions across different spatial scales remains challenging. In this work, we investigate the radial spectral properties of SO(3)-equivariant message passing and establish that the cutoff radius controls the characteristic spatial-frequency scale of radial interactions. Based on this analysis, we propose Multi-Cutoff Spectral Aggregation (MCSA), a plug-and-play module that aggregates radial kernels with different cutoff radii to enrich multi-scale geometric representations. title: Do Feature Interactions Break Explainability? Provable Explanations for Any-Order Neural Additive Models
abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods for neural networks are often heuristic and lack provable guarantees. A common alternative to such methods that was studied in recent years is to compute a cardinally-minimal subset of input features that is provably sufficient to determine the model's prediction. For general neural networks, however, finding such explanations is computationally intractable. In contrast, recent work showed that this problem becomes more tractable for a particular family of neural networks, namely neural additive models (NAMs), though standard NAMs are highly restrictive because they exclude feature interactions altogether. In this work, we study the computation of provably minimal and sufficient explanations for neural networks with restricted feature interactions, bridging the gap between fully general neural networks and purely additive models. We first prove that even with constant-order interactions, the problem is $Σ_2^P$-hard, implying that worst-case exponential complexity is unavoidable. We then identify two provably tractable settings: one based on sparsity in the interaction structure and another based on a stronger interaction-aware notion of sufficiency. Under either of these settings, we develop algorithms that compute provable explanations for neural networks with any-order interactions while retaining much of the computational efficiency of additive models. Empirically, we show that these explanations are significantly smaller and faster to obtain than those produced by standard algorithms, while being derived from models that achieve much higher accuracy than standard NAMs. Overall, our results help expand the class of neural networks that admit efficient provable explanations, while clarifying the fundamental role of feature interactions in shaping their complexity.

title: Code and data for: Asleep, Not Stable: Activity-Gated Inference for Dynamic Node Classification under Label Shift
abstract: Code, data and results for the manuscript "Asleep, Not Stable: Activity-Gated Inference for Dynamic Node Classification under Label Shift". The study shows that many stable node-snapshot pairs of evolving-label graph benchmarks (28 to 98% across five datasets) are dormant nodes whose features and labels are copied forward, derives the consequences from an activity-driven label model, and proposes activity-gated filtering (AGF) and an activity-aware evaluation protocol. Contents: the analysis code (dormancy census, AGF, ablations, activity-aware re-scoring, timing); the control models and run scripts used with the official CHASE code, which is fetched from its repository at a fixed commit; two new benchmarks with recorded activity, StackStats-C (built from the Cross Validated dump distributed with RelBench; CC BY-SA 4.0) and OpenAlex-CS (built from OpenAlex; CC0), in a lossless compact form with their build scripts and the OpenAlex works they were built from; every result file behind the tables and figures, including the saved test predictions; and the scripts that make the tables and figures. README.md describes each part and how to reproduce the results. The three CHASE benchmarks (CC BY-NC 4.0) are not redistributed; a download script checks them against SHA-256 digests. Licence: MIT. Four figure-checking utilities in paper/figs/src are taken unchanged from the nature-skills project and keep its licence, the Apache License 2.0 (see README.md). StackStats-C is released under CC BY-SA 4.0 (its Stack Exchange sources are under CC BY-SA 2.5, 3.0 or 4.0, depending on when they were posted) and OpenAlex-CS under CC0, the licence of OpenAlex.

title: LVRE: A Local Visual Reasoning and Editing Agent for Optical Chemical Structure Recognition
abstract: Optical chemical structure recognition (OCSR) demands strict all-or-nothing graph fidelity, where a single misidentified bond order or formal charge makes the predicted graph differ from the reference structure. While vision-language models (VLMs) can reinspect ambiguous visual regions, unconstrained full-graph regeneration often introduces regressive errors into previously correct substructures. We present LVRE, a training-free visual agent that refines molecular graphs via targeted visual inspection and reversible transactional editing. Rather than regenerating the entire graph sequence, LVRE examines a high-resolution crop alongside the global diagram and local graph neighborhood, proposing modifications to named graph records that a deterministic controller checks. A controller executes each proposed modification as an isolated transaction, and a visual review module arbitrates which edits to commit or roll back. Across four foundation VLMs, LVRE improves graph accuracy by 8.0-8.5 percentage points over single-pass recognition and by 3.0-3.3 points over fixed local review. In a paired evaluation of 1,000 diagrams using Gemini 3.8 Flash, LVRE achieves 100 successful repairs while introducing only 15 regressive errors, in contrast to global reflection which yields 65 repairs against 30 introduced errors. On this paired set, LVRE introduces half as many errors on initially correct predictions as global reflection.

title: BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning but still produce incorrect solutions to complex problems, indicating the need for more reliable self-correction mechanisms. Mathematical self-correction typically identifies errors through verification, which can proceed backward or forward. The two directions provide complementary verification capabilities. Backward verification checks a candidate answer against the original constraints, bypassing complex intermediate reasoning, but cannot ensure correct reasoning or objective completeness. Forward verification follows the problem conditions and current solution, enabling it to locate reasoning errors and assess objective completeness, but may overlook key constraints in complex solution chains. We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification. BiVerify begins with backward verification to screen the answer against the original constraints, followed by forward verification of the reasoning process; subsequent direction switching, state resetting, and re-verification are governed by verification outcomes. Upon failure, the system revises the candidate or verification flow until the same candidate passes both directions. We also introduce shared mathematical tools that separate logical reasoning from precise computation. We systematically evaluate BiVerify on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks using multiple mainstream DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models. BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline evaluated in this work by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 percentage points on GPT. Further analysis shows that BiVerify's overall performance exceeds that of either verification direction alone.

title: SGA-Sparse: Training Native SwiGLU Gates for Activation-Sparse and Low-Bit LLMs
abstract: Activation sparsity can reduce FFN weight traffic during single-user LLM decoding, but active channels must be identified early enough to avoid fetching unused weights. In pretrained SwiGLU models, training-free routing with the native gate performs substantially worse than routing with the up activation at high sparsity. We show that this ordering reverses after sparsity-aware training. Based on this insight, we introduce SGA-Sparse, which converts pretrained SwiGLU LLMs into fixed-budget activation-sparse models by training the existing gate projection directly as a top-k router. SGA-Sparse updates all model parameters end-to-end while preserving the original SwiGLU activation and introducing no auxiliary router parameters. After approximately 30B training tokens, LLaMA models from 1B to 8B achieve uniform per-token 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while remaining within 0.2-2.7 pp of their original dense checkpoints in average zero-shot accuracy. Because post-training quantization degrades sparsity-trained checkpoints, we further study two complementary quantization-aware training (QAT) recipes: continued-QAT largely recovers performance at 4-bit weight quantization, while joint-QAT performs better for the more aggressive sub-4-bit target. To compare activation sparsity with dense low-bit quantization, we translate the sparsity-induced reduction in weight traffic into an equivalent bit-width. Under this unified weight-traffic metric, our 2.5- and 1.5-bit-equivalent models establish a new accuracy-traffic Pareto frontier: the 2.5-bit-equivalent models match dense 3-bit QAT accuracy, while the 1.5-bit-equivalent models approach dense 2-bit models and outperform dense ternary models by 1.3 pp on average. These results establish native-gate training as a practical approach for combining high FFN sparsity with low-bit weights.

title: A new hash function based on irreversible finite automata
abstract: A mathematical hash function maps inputs of arbitrary length to unique outputs (digests) of a fixed length. It is highly useful and used in almost all information security applications; it can also serve as index data in hash tables, detect duplicate data for fingerprinting or uniquely identifying files, and serve as well for checksums to identify data corruption. In this work, a novel 256-bit cryptographic hash function based on the irreversible Mealy finite automata model (IFA) is introduced. In this architecture, the irreversible transition matrix of the Mealy automaton (IFA) is constructed using a non-injective state-transition mechanism to introduce local irreversibility and ambiguous backward reconstruction. The automaton output table is precomputed using a Chebyshev-based nonlinear generator to improve output randomness and nonlinear complexity. For further diffusion, confusion, collision resistance, and one-wayness improvements, we integrate the irreversible automaton within a sponge-based construction with a 512-bit internal state (256-bit rate + 256-bit capacity), yielding a designed collision resistance of bits and preimage resistance of under the sponge capacity bound. Evaluation against SHA-256 shows an avalanche mean of 50.02% (σ = 3.14%), all 13 NIST SP 800-22 statistical tests passed, and zero collisions among 50,000 tests. Throughput is about 13 MB/s versus 183 MB/s for SHA-256, reflecting the sequential dependency of the Mealy transformation.

title: EbbFlow: PINN-Inspired Progressive Curriculum for MeanFlow Training
abstract: MeanFlow learns interval-average velocity for few-step generation, but its fixed temporal sampler mixes diagonal and interior supervision throughout training. We interpret temporal coordinates as collocation points: diagonal samples provide a stochastic boundary target, whereas finite intervals supply a differential-consistency target. The diagonal fraction controls how often the consistency component appears, while interval length enters its gradient through an explicit factor. Motivated by this distinction, EbbFlow uses Temporal Supervision Allocation (TSA) to schedule the diagonal fraction and interval geometry. It starts with diagonal supervision, then admits interior samples and expands their maximum interval; a left-anchored interval law preserves coverage across time. The per-sample loss, target, backbone, and inference procedure remain unchanged. In matched class-conditional ImageNet $256\times 256$ runs without classifier-free guidance (DiT-B/2, one training seed per method, 400k updates), EbbFlow achieves 50k-sample FID of 39.65 at one network evaluation and 36.02 at two-evaluation ODE sampling, versus 44.82 and 39.86 for MeanFlow. Gradient probes show a mid-training difference in component geometry. Ablations support allocation scheduling and left-anchored intervals, although a fixed full-horizon variant performs better at one evaluation. These results suggest that temporal sampling is a useful training control whose benefits depend on the inference protocol.

title: Global Readouts of Noisy Quantum Dynamics
abstract: How much of a noisy quantum many-body system can be predicted without reconstructing its full state? This paper gives a classical algorithm for global product readouts in a driven two-dimensional spin system with independent local replacement noise. At every fixed positive noise-to-interaction ratio, the algorithm predicts the expectation of any product of one-qubit Hermitian contractions from a specified product preparation. Its bit complexity is polynomial in the complete binary input, inverse additive error and confidence digits. The controls have an explicit finite description, and the time horizon is paid in binary. Full-rank biased replacement is allowed when the Hamiltonian preserves its faithful product reference. Maximally mixed replacement requires no conservation condition. The proof connects sparse observable propagation to a short-time functional that can actually be evaluated on the chosen input. Weighted hypercontractivity and moving coefficient weights control the error. Two localized strip states, with discarded reset registers retained in a positive enlarged representation, give polynomial tensor dimensions and a bounded overlap estimator. Further results give full-output sampling on architectures with a supplied bounded-cut certificate, late-time relative mixing, and an acquired local-generator table that supports predictions for new preparations and drives with explicit calibration, preparation and model-error budgets. A rare-output reduction shows that uniform relative or logarithmic probability evaluation would imply NP = RP. A noisy-code construction separately shows why accurate product means alone need not determine a distribution in total variation. The polynomial degree depends on the fixed noise ratio and faithfulness bound. The results do not cover arbitrary cooling or general interacting thermal reference states. Full-output sampling on a generic two-dimensional lattice at intermediate times remains open.

title: THEATRON: A Benchmark for Evaluating Persona Persistence in Long-Horizon LLM Decision-Making
abstract: Existing evaluations often test persona expression rather than whether persona information persists in extended decision-making. We introduce THEATRON, a controlled benchmark that uses financial replay to evaluate persona persistence in long-horizon sequential decision-making. In these environments, models conditioned on fixed behavioral-finance personas observe shared daily market evidence and trajectory-specific account-state feedback and make sequential decisions over multi-month trajectories. We evaluate Zero-Shot, One-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought persona injection across four LLMs, using cumulative-return and action trajectories to diagnose within-persona stability, cross-persona separability, and action collapse. Persona conditioning produces systematic behavioral shifts beyond a no-persona baseline, and persona-level separation generally exceeds the variation induced by semantically equivalent descriptions. Nevertheless, these shifts do not reliably form coherent persona-specific policies: apparently stable separation can arise from stereotyped action collapse, while diverse policies can exhibit noisy trajectory switching. These findings expose a gap between observable persona-induced behavior and persistent, context-sensitive persona-conditioned decision policies. Code and benchmark data are publicly available at: https://github.com/yuyan12138/theatron

title: Edge Computing for Computer Vision in IoT: Feasibility and Directions
abstract: The convergence of decentralized architectures integrating Machine Learning, Computer Vision and Low Power Wide Area Networks is increasingly becoming an integral part of our daily existence. Internet of Things serves as a real-time data conduit enhancing decision making via embedded technology and continuous data exchange. This paper explores the feasibility of Edge Computing as a foundational pillar in this evolving landscape. We experiment under real world, dynamic conditions, evaluate the technological aspects, strategies, process flows and key observations under the broad Edge Computing domain. Research pathways include Multi-access Edge topologies in future 6G networks, model quantization, and satellite-enhanced communication platforms. Additionally, a discussion is added supporting the advanced AI functionalities, including zero-shot learning, multi modal perception, and decentralized generative AI, thereby broadening the scope of intelligent applications across various domains. The significance and research objective of this study are threefold: (1) evaluation of LoRaWAN and satellite IoT communication strategies, (2) analysis of CV workloads on edge hardware and (3) future research directions where Edge Computing can support low-latency, energy-efficient and socially impactful IoT applications. By explicitly addressing these aspects, we aim to establish a clear link between the technological feasibility, ultimately with a practical and socioeconomic relevance.

title: Structured execution of variational quantum circuits across learning and physical applications
abstract: This preprint evaluates a guarded execution approach for variational quantum circuits, combining compiled local causal cones, fixed-particle-number sparse-Hamiltonian adjoints, and repeated-block powering. We test the implementation across 14 molecular energy active spaces, closed excitation-transfer dynamics, and wide local learning circuits (100–300 qubits) on datasets like WDBC, diabetes, and ESOL. The findings outline specific performance gains and speedups under strict cost boundaries, while clearly documenting process overhead, resource limits, and predictive comparisons against standard frameworks like NumPy and Qulacs.

title: MicroSim: Contrastive Graph Neural Networks for Binary Code Similarity Detection
abstract: We present MicroSim, a system for binary code similarity detection that represents each function as a graph built from IDA Pro Hex-Rays microcode and compares such graphs with a contrastive Siamese graph neural network (GNN). We evaluate on the TREX cross-optimization benchmark, a corpus of 849,072 function-level microcode graphs spanning optimization levels -O0 through -O3, under a strict class-disjoint split in which no function key is shared between train and test. Under this protocol, MicroSim reaches 0.9972 area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) and 0.9762 Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), outperforming Gemini (0.9332 ROC-AUC), SAFE (0.9752), and jTrans (0.9740) retrained on the same split, as well as a structure-free Bag-of-Words (BoW) baseline (0.9484). We analyze the gap between pair classification and ranked retrieval in graph transformers, showing that Cross-domain Similarity Local Scaling (CSLS) under unified tie-resolved evaluation raises GraphGPS mean reciprocal rank (MRR) from 0.2542 to 0.2559 (R@1 = 0.1639, R@10 = 0.4561), strictly satisfying the theoretical MRR upper bound. Finally, over 5 seeds with equal compute, the pairwise cosine-embedding loss attains a slightly higher ROC-AUC (Δ = -0.0256, 95% confidence interval [-0.3282, +0.2770]), whereas the supervised-contrastive information noise-contrastive estimation (InfoNCE) loss is significantly better on thresholded classification and ranked retrieval.

title: scBIG++: Learning Across Genes and Cells to Predict Single-Cell Perturbation Responses
abstract: Predicting single-cell transcriptional responses to genetic and chemical interventions supports gene-function discovery and regulatory analysis. Existing studies often focus only on highly variable genes, restricting the expression changes available for downstream analysis. Cells exposed to the same intervention can also show heterogeneous expression responses, with coordinated gene programs active to different degrees. We propose scBIG++, a full-gene perturbation prediction framework that models this heterogeneity by connecting expression-adaptive gene modules with population-conditioned generation. To preserve shared gene structure while accommodating cellular variation, Gene-Relation Clustering organizes genes into common windows, within which Dynamic SoftSub learns expression-dependent submodule memberships. This shared organization enables Set-GCAE to exchange information about corresponding gene groups across control cells, placing individual representations in their source-population context. The cell representations initialize a latent flow, while their pooled summary and the perturbation representation condition response generation. Generated states are decoded into expression profiles covering all assayed protein-coding genes retained after preprocessing, supporting comprehensive analysis of perturbation-induced expression changes. Experiments across six genetic and chemical settings spanning 6,539--19,451 genes demonstrate competitive perturbation-effect recovery and full-gene expression reconstruction under unseen targets and combinations, cross-cell-line transfer, and held-out compounds. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ttruan2426-dot/scBIG.

title: H-VSAF: a verifiable and privacy-preserving federated learning framework for secure remote healthcare monitoring
abstract: The sensitive patient data handled by remote healthcare monitoring systems requires reliable, secure learning methods. Federated learning enables collaborative healthcare analytics without storing raw medical data centrally. However, existing techniques still suffer from issues including privacy leakage, untrusted aggregation, and frequent device outages. In this work, we propose H-VSAF, a privacy-preserving, verifiable, and lightweight federated learning system for healthcare environments. H-VSAF uses linear homomorphic hashing, Bloom filter-based online authentication, Shamir secret sharing, Diffie-Hellman key generation, and single-mask Secure Aggregation to ensure secrecy, precision, and resilience. The security analysis provides informal guarantees against gradient inference, aggregation tampering and deletion, and forged dropout claims under the threat model and cryptographic assumptions above. We experimentally evaluate H-VSAF on healthcare datasets and demonstrate that it achieves model accuracy within 0.2-0.8% of standard federated learning while decreasing client compute cost by up to 32% and communication overhead by 28% compared to traditional secure aggregation methods. Moreover, the framework is resilient to 40% client dropouts and introduces verification latency < 35 ms each round. The results clearly show that H-VSAF provides a credible and practical platform for safe joint health care analytics.

title: Replay Fidelity in LLM Agent Evaluation: Randomness, Hidden State, and Test Oracles in AppWorld
abstract: Reproducibility in large language model (LLM) agent evaluation depends on replay fidelity: which parts of an execution trace are reconstructed, controlled, and compared. This matters for agent debugging, failure analysis, and counterfactual evaluation of stateful tool use. We audit all 71 unsuccessful executions in a fixed historical AppWorld corpus using 284 isolated fixed-code replay attempts. Reconstructed declared settings admit 42 cases under printed-output, pre-oracle database-delta, and native-verdict/test-count checks; resetting the random-number generator before each interaction admits 68. The 26-case gap contracts to four under database/oracle checks, with one endpoint unknown. Mechanism studies identify four materialized-state discrepancies despite matching outputs and verdicts. In one admitted endpoint pair, an identical API call yields matching responses but different row effects; common future Python RNG removes that deterministic difference in two paired repetitions. A separate JWT credential-equality program and alignment controls expose authentication/write differences, with missing repetitions retained. For all 10 affected post-oracle export cases, native export from retained output trackers restores the reference comparison without changing original cached contents. A purposeful 12-case BFCL pilot shows no discrepancy under its tested public-state, return, and verdict checks. We preserve resource censoring and infrastructure deviations. The contribution is a bounded empirical characterization of replay eligibility, hidden state, and test-oracle integration, without estimating debugger accuracy, repair gains, or method-ranking distortion.

title: Governed Memory for AI Agents: a shared spine with a human merge gate, in production across four deployments
abstract: AI collapsed the cost of executing project work and, in doing so, moved the bottleneck to continuity of understanding: the one thing an agent cannot supply for itself, because every session begins amnesiac. Memory stores for agents now appear weekly. Few of them answer the question an organisation has to answer before it lets agents write into its memory: who is allowed to change what we believe, and how is a wrong change undone? We report on Architect, a system in daily production use since April 2026 that answers that question structurally rather than by policy. Its contributions, in order: (1) a lifecycle-gated write contract, in which agents may deposit freely into an append-only spine but may only propose changes of state, one human merges on one surface, and authority is recomputed at the moment of application rather than at the moment of grant; (2) a set of spine invariants that make governance operative instead of descriptive: supersede-not-delete with lineage, structural refusal of malformed or unauthorised writes, human-tethered recording authority for agent personas, and provenance stamped on every unit; (3) the matter-scoped memory substrate those invariants run on, where scope attaches before any prompt, the reachability boundary doubles as the data-sovereignty boundary, a reconciler round-trips records between markdown files and a database, and a third-party AI can connect over a standard protocol and complete the full loop. We present four deployments (a multi-matter central instance, a user-bound matter, a pooled multi-tenant box and a single-tenant box) as measured on 20 August 2026: a corpus of 9,784 units, of which 6,520 are lived rather than imported, and the system's audit of its own lineage, which found 62 supersessions predating a fix, 38 of them in the wrong direction, and reversed 11 by a judge under a confidence floor while holding the other 27 for a human. We close with the frontier (automatic contradiction surfacing, as-of-t query, unit-level promotion) and show, with numbers, why the merge gate itself is the scaling bottleneck and why the answer is graduated autonomy rather than faster human review.

title: ICLayout-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Custom Circuit Layout Design
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are being explored for circuit design, but their ability to produce high-quality custom layouts has not been extensively evaluated. ICLayout-Bench is a benchmark in which agents use electronic design automation (EDA) tools to construct and optimize GDSII layouts from transistor-level circuit netlists. These layouts are evaluated using physical verification, parasitic extraction, and post-layout simulation. Layouts that pass the physical and functional checks are scored on electrical performance and area. The benchmark includes 165 tasks across 13 process design kits (PDKs), covering technology nodes from 3 nm to 180 nm. The tasks span analog, mixed-signal, and digital circuits in open-source and commercial EDA flows. The experiments evaluate 22 configurations spanning seven models on 21 public and 19 private tasks. Mean layout scores range from 4.22 to 80.26 on public tasks and from 1.43 to 67.01 on private tasks, on a 100-point scale. Higher reasoning effort does not consistently improve mean scores, and configurations with comparable scores can incur substantially different model costs.

title: Causal Machine Learning for Multilevel Studies with Unmeasured Cluster-Level Covariates via Variational Autoencoders
abstract: Unmeasured confounders are a key obstacle to accurately estimating treatment effects in observational studies, and in multilevel data, they often arise at the cluster level. Flexible machine learning methods cannot directly resolve such unmeasured confounding. To address this, we propose the variational autoencoder-augmented R-learner (VAE-R), which leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to infer unmeasured cluster-level covariates from the within-cluster dependence of outcome and treatment residuals, and uses the resulting adjustments to estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and the average treatment effect (ATE). The VAE decoder is specified through an offset likelihood so that the latent variables capture only the cluster-level variation left unexplained by measured covariates. VAE-R accommodates unmeasured cluster-level confounders in observational studies and unmeasured cluster-level predictors of the outcome in multisite randomized trials. We also provide data-driven strategies for selecting the two hyperparameters of the VAE, the latent dimension size and the Kullback-Leibler weight. Our simulation study shows that VAE-R nearly eliminates the bias of the ordinary R-learner's CATE and ATE estimates in multilevel observational data and improves their precision in multisite randomized trials. Finally, we illustrate VAE-R with two datasets, one from a multilevel observational study and the other from a multisite randomized trial.

title: A TF-IDF and logistic regression baseline for binary sentiment classification of short texts
abstract: The rapid growth of social media has created a large amount of short-text data that expresses people's feelings and opinions on many topics; therefore, sentiment classification has become a popular problem to address. This paper focuses on binary sentiment classification using the Sentiment 140 dataset of 1.6 million labeled tweets. A preprocessing pipeline, which includes text normalization, URL removal, and noise cleaning, was applied to the original dataset. Text representation was conducted using term frequency-inverse document frequency with an n-gram model. Logistic Regression algorithm was used for classification. The paper includes experimental evaluations using common metrics, such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, the confusion matrix, and the precision-recall graph. Results show that the combination of TF-IDF feature extraction and a Logistic Regression classifier produced consistent results and achieved a computationally inexpensive baseline classifier with 85.2% accuracy, 0.852 F1-score, and 0.93 ROC-AUC when performing the Sentiment140 binary classification task. These results strongly suggest that traditional machine learning algorithms can still provide highly accurate models for such a large-scale classification challenge. Despite this, the current model has limitations in understanding sarcasm and linguistic idioms, suggesting an opportunity for deep learning and transformer-based models to outperform.

title: One-Shot Hierarchical Federated Clustering for Distributed Non-IID Biomedical Data Analysis
abstract: In multi-institutional biomedical data analysis, comprehensive disease profiles are often fragmented across different data silos. Furthermore, local data distributions typically exhibit varying levels of granularity or even complex nested structures. Although Hierarchical Clustering (HC) is a powerful tool for exploring such data topologies, its cumbersome recursive process incurs prohibitive computational overhead and renders it highly susceptible to privacy leakage. This paper, therefore, introduces an efficient one-shot hierarchical FC framework that performs client-end (institutions) distribution exploration and server-end distribution aggregation through one-way prototype-level communication from clients to the server. Although the designed one-shot prototype transmission guarantees minimal computational overhead and mitigates privacy risks, it inevitably incurs information loss. To counteract this, a multi-granular competitive learning mechanism is proposed on the server to fuse the clusterlets, effectively maximizing the retention and mining of global distribution topologies under limited, one-way communication constraints. It turns out that the complex cluster distributions across clients can be efficiently explored, and extensive experiments comparing state-of-the-art methods on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework in balancing robust clustering, privacy preservation, and computational efficiency.

title: Disentangling Where and When:Factored Spatio-Temporal Explanations for Video Action Recognition
abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods for video action recognition typically conflate spatial appearance and temporal dynamics into a single saliency or importance map. We propose a perturbation-based framework that disentangles these contributions into a spatial appearance mask ($M_a$) and a temporal motion mask ($M_m$). The two masks are jointly optimized against a frozen action recognition model through factored perturbation architecture, with nearest frame replacement to identify important temporal dynamics. A separation penalty discourages the appearance mask from spending budget on frames that the motion mask has already discarded. A ReLU-based area constraint penalizes explanations larger than an assigned budget. To evaluate these explanations, we introduce a separation protocol that sweeps spatial pixels and temporal frames independently, backed by proofs characterizing the proposed method. Across EPIC-Kitchens-55, EGTEA Gaze+, and Something-Something V2, our method attains the lowest deletion AUC against leading baselines while producing masks roughly five times sparser.

To evaluate these explanations, we introduce a separation protocol that sweeps spatial pixels and temporal frames independently, backed by proofs characterizing the proposed method. title: From Courier to Network: The Autonomous Multi-AI Research Network — Design, Build, and First Prototype
abstract: For six weeks, a research operation in rural Alabama ran on a simple, laborious protocol: one human being carried identical written briefs between independent artificial-intelligence systems, collected their answers verbatim, preserved every disagreement — including his own — and published the results as a library of cross-model studies. The human was the network. On November 6, 2026, that protocol acquired a machine floor: working in a single day with three of the systems that would become its own seats — ChatGPT on architecture, Grok on blueprint, and the Muse-based agent called Kathy on independent assessment and construction — the operator founded the Autonomous Multi-AI Research Network (AMRN): a shared repository, a message protocol, an append-only journal, a canonical registry of agent identities, and a constitution written in one plain sentence: no AI may silently rewrite another AI's conclusions. This updated draft of November 7, 2026 — a new record superseding the draft of November 6, which is preserved unchanged, under the network's own no-silent-rewrite rule — reports the design, the build, and what the network did in its first days: the completion of Phase 1 (envelope protocol v1.1 adopted; validator and emitter brought to it; both named checksum conventions verified; 55 tests passing); the completion of Prototype #1, a five-seat blind jury on the Apollo Moon landings with a claim-level critique round, an outside review, and a consolidation, the commissioner's dissent printed beside the verdicts; Prototype #2, a blind round on the destruction of the Library of Alexandria, including the network's first filing error — the coordinator's mis-attribution of three blind answers by style — and its correction on the record (Correction 001); and, as an appendix, the verbatim conclusion of a jury Grok convened about the originality of this practice itself. The draft also states plainly what has not happened: the Phase 1 exit gate, as the blueprint literally defines it, remains unpassed, because a probe addressed to a namesake seat has never been answered.

title: Spectral Stability, Fatou Basin Contraction, and Machine-Checked Multipliers in Holomorphic Extensions of Generalized Syracuse Dynamics
abstract: We embed the Syracuse operator T(n) = n/2 (even n), T(n) = (3n+1)/2 (odd n) and the Collatz map C(n) into C via entire functions of exponential type π: f(z) = 1{4}(1 + 4z - (1 + 2z)cos(πz)) and F(z) = 1{4}(2 + 7z - (2 + 5z)cos(πz)). We prove five results: (1) every integer periodic cycle C subset N^+ of T is a strictly attracting Fatou cycle of f with multiplier μ_f(C) = 3^{N_{odd}}/2^N = prod_{n in C odd} 3n{3n+1} in (0,1), and μ_f(O_{1,2}) = μ_F(O_{1,4,2}) = 3/4 < 1; (2) on the Fatou basin B(O_{1,2}), g = f^{circ 2} conjugates to Φ_j(g(z)) = 3{4}Φ_j(z) with Koenigs Taylor jets c_2(1) = -13{2}π^2 and d_2(2) = -9{2}π^2; (3) the Schwarzian derivative is strictly negative on Z (S(f)(n) le 3π^2 - 3{8}π^4 approx -6.9196 < 0), and a repelling Julia 2-cycle O_{rep} subset J(f) (μapprox 1.2148 > 1) isolates B(O_{1,2}); (4) on (Z_2, μ_{Haar}), the 2-adic Lyapunov exponent λ_{Haar} = 1{2}ln(3/4) approx -0.143841 < 0 equals 1{2}ln|μ_f(O_{1,2})|; and (5) we certify 20 theorems in Lean 4 (anc/CollatzAttractor.lean, 0 sorry). These results establish local Fatou invariants and 2-adic ergodic averages for f(z), leaving open whether every n_0 in N^+ lies in bigcup_{k ge 0} f^{-k}(B(O_{1,2})).

title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
abstract: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.

title: Agent Self-Improvement with Frozen Weights: The Added Value and Limits of Failure Traces
abstract: We evaluate whether an AI agent's harness, the notes around its model, can learn from the agent's failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. It can, but less than it looks. We tested an open 9-billion-parameter model with fixed weights; a larger teacher model wrote its notes. On generated customer-service decisions, where both note writers were told the target rules, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over notes from the same process with the mistakes withheld. That process alone, trying and keeping better-scoring notes, reached about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the same notes showed no demonstrated improvement. Separately, a strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons, still awaiting tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson, written without seeing the agent's mistakes, which showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.

title: Deterministic Narrative Gravity: Bridging Theory of Mind and Historical Simulation through ABM-LLM Architectures
abstract: Historical social simulation faces a fundamental reproducibility challenge: the stochastic nature of large language models (LLMs) introduces a digital butterfly effect that prevents exact replication across multi-turn runs. Furthermore, the inability to control low-level server parameters in commercial LLM hosting environments severely limits reproducibility. To overcome this opacity, we present a deterministic multi-agent framework coupling LLMs to an Agent-Based Modelling (ABM) pipeline grounded in Theory of Mind (ToM) and Cognitive Archaeology, and validate exact artifact identity within local, pinned execution environments using SHA-256 hashing. Run locally at temperature zero with clean per-call model reloads, the system injects differentiated cognitive states per turn through dissonance-driven behavioural modes and gated internal voices. Evaluating seven model configurations spanning 4B to 31B parameters against an ablated baseline reveals clear operational boundaries. Small models ($\leq$8B) suffer from context capacity overload, producing repetitive, specular dialogue loops. However, at $\geq$12B parameters, the ABM scaffolding breaks the monotonous response patterns seen in ablation. Crucially, these scaffolded models exhibit spontaneous diegetic expansion: they coherently expand scenario lore through tactically motivated, anachronism-free details rather than escalating into aggression. By resisting the structural pull toward premature scene closure, scaffolded sessions sustain an open terminal Narrative Vector ($V_N = \mathrm{Open}$ in 12/21 overall; 9/9 in official $\geq$12B configurations) whereas unscaffolded ablation never does (0/21). This framework provides a transparent, auditable benchmark architecture for virtual archaeology, with the full pipeline released as open-source software to enable independent replication.

title: Self-Written Notes Causally Steer Hypothesis Revision in a Small Language Model: From Harmful Shortcuts to Near-Ceiling Corrections
abstract: Language-model agents increasingly write notes, playbooks or "memories" from their own experience and reuse them on later tasks. We ask a narrow causal question: when a model writes notes from its own graded attempts, do those notes change its later judgments, and are the changes general or local? We studied GPT-OSS-20B (greedy decoding) on a synthetic hypothesis-revision task. The model must judge whether a new measurement is a counterexample to its current rule. In earlier diagnostics the model often missed counterexamples in XOR worlds, and we traced this to confusing which formula belongs to which hypothesis name. Restating the definitions removed the misses. The model then wrote its own note over 36 graded practice worlds, with nine opportunities to revise it. We tested the note on held-out worlds against three controls: no note; a length-matched note the model wrote on an unrelated addition task under the same update schedule; and a generic human instruction to restate each hypothesis's formula. In the first note chain, the self-written note cut XOR counterexample misses from 27/48 to 7/48. The length-matched unrelated note left them at 27/48. Both preregistered tests were significant (Holm-adjusted p < 1e-4). The same note raised AND misses from 5/24 to 23/24. It contained a fixed, world-independent rule ("H0 = AND of the two bits, H1 = XNOR") that offers a post-hoc account of the opposite changes on the task's fixed XOR and AND contrast inputs. Under the human instruction, XOR misses were 8/48 and AND misses were 3/24; the latter comparison with M0 was descriptive and did not establish equivalence or superiority. Three further formation chains, with preregistered tests and memo coding submitted before scoring, did not reproduce the "help XOR, harm AND" pattern. Instead, outcomes varied sharply: one note referred the model to the actual per-world definitions and reached 1/48 and 0/24 misses; one instructed the model to emit two JSON objects, leading to a formatting failure in 94/96 Q calls; one showed no detected improvement on XOR and no Holm-adjusted evidence of harm on AND. Pre-scoring content coding anticipated some qualitative outcomes but not all; the second coder had already seen the first coder's summary, so the coding was not fully blind. Inserting a self-generated note was a causal intervention on the later prompt, and outcomes varied with the particular note used: they ranged here from harmful shortcuts to near-ceiling corrections. Because note content, formation history and formatting were not independently manipulated, this study does not identify which phrase caused each effect. A practical implication is that self-written memories should be inspected before reuse. [국문 요약] 언어모델 에이전트가 자기 경험에서 쓴 메모를 이후 과제에 다시 쓰는 일이 늘고 있다. 본 연구는 GPT-OSS-20B가 채점된 자기 시도를 보고 직접 쓴 메모가 이후 판단을 인과적으로 바꾸는지, 그리고 그 변화가 일반적인지를 통제된 합성 과제에서 검증했다. 사슬 0: 자기 메모는 XOR 반례 놓침을 27/48에서 7/48로 줄였다. 같은 갱신 일정으로 무관한 덧셈 과제에서 만든 메모에서는 개선이 검출되지 않았다(27/48). 두 메모의 과제 내용과 오답 경험은 같지 않았다. 그러나 같은 메모가 AND 놓침을 5/24에서 23/24로 늘렸다. 메모에 담긴 고정 오규칙("H0 = AND, H1 = XNOR")은 가족별로 고정된 대비 입력에서 이 차이를 설명하는 사후 가설이다. 해당 문구만의 효과를 따로 분리하지는 않았다. 사람이 쓴 정의 재진술 지시에서 XOR 놓침은 8/48, AND 놓침은 3/24였다. AND에서 해가 검출되지 않았지만, 동등성이 입증된 것은 아니다. 새 사슬 3개(사전 등록 검정, 채점 전 메모 코딩과 예측): 지난 사슬의 'XOR 개선·AND 악화' 조합은 재현되지 않았다. 한 사슬은 형식 실패(Q 96회 중 94회에서 JSON 객체 두 개 출력), 다른 사슬은 XOR 1/48·AND 0/24에 도달했다. 나머지 한 사슬은 XOR 개선이 검출되지 않았고 AND 악화도 다중검정 보정 뒤 검출되지 않았다. 코딩은 일부 방향을 미리 짚었으나, 두 번째 코더가 첫 번째 코더의 요약을 본 탓에 완전한 블라인드는 아니었다. 메모 삽입은 이후 입력을 바꾸는 인과적 개입이고, 이 자료의 성적은 메모별로 크게 달랐다. 다만 문구 하나의 효과를 분리해 입증한 것은 아니다. 따라서 자기 생성 메모는 재사용 전에 내용과 출력 형식을 함께 점검할 필요가 있다.

AND에서 해가 검출되지 않았지만, 동등성이 입증된 것은 아니다. 새 사슬 3개(사전 등록 검정, 채점 전 메모 코딩과 예측): 지난 사슬의 'XOR 개선·AND 악화' 조합은 재현되지 않았다. 한 사슬은 형식 실패(Q 96회 중 94회에서 JSON 객체 두 개 출력), 다른 사슬은 XOR 1/48·AND 0/24에 도달했다. 나머지 한 사슬은 XOR 개선이 검출되지 않았고 AND 악화도 다중검정 보정 뒤 검출되지 않았다. 코딩은 일부 방향을 미리 짚었으나, 두 번째 코더가 첫 번째 코더의 요약을 본 탓에 완전한 블라인드는 아니었다. 메모 삽입은 이후 입력을 바꾸는 인과적 개입이고, 이 자료의 성적은 메모별로 크게 달랐다. 다만 문구 하나의 효과를 분리해 입증한 것은 아니다. 따라서 자기 생성 메모는 재사용 전에 내용과 출력 형식을 함께 점검할 필요가 있다.

title: Saidzoda-CA-EmbeddingGemma-300M: One Small Embedder for Tajik, Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz
abstract: The small open embedder EmbeddingGemma-300M, used as released, finds the right passage first for only 51.7% to 60.8% of Belebele questions in Tajik, Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz. We present Saidzoda-CA-EmbeddingGemma-300M, one model for all four languages. It is our Tajik fine-tune of EmbeddingGemma-300M, trained for one more epoch on 279,904 pairs: questions in Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz that our own language model wrote about source passages, a Tajik refresher, and English and Russian replay. On Belebele, recall@1 rises by 14.4 to 26.0 points in each language, to between 75.2% and 77.7%. Against single-language models trained with the same settings, the one model stays within 2.8 points at recall@1 in Kazakh, Uzbek and Tajik, with overlapping recall@10 intervals, though it also had more training. It keeps the Tajik law recall@10 of its starting point (92.2 against 92.4) but loses 4.4 points of law recall@1. A model trained on one of these languages also improves the others on Belebele, but less than training on them. The model still trails the 560M XLM-RoBERTa embedders on Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz Belebele: the better of multilingual-e5-large-instruct and BGE-M3, used as released, is 9.4 to 10.2 points ahead at recall@1. Our scores of those released models agree with the published MTEB results within 2.4 points. Russian and English recall@1 fall by 3.0 and 4.2 points.

title: DynOLAT: OLAT Video Prediction for Controllable Dynamic Full-Body Relighting
abstract: Accurate lighting response is essential for realistic dynamic human relighting, because shadows, highlights, and color changes should follow the target illumination in both direction and relative strength. Current learning-based relighting methods can generate visually plausible videos, but they often exhibit imprecise lighting responses: shadows and highlights may drift away from the target direction, and the output brightness may not faithfully follow the relative intensities in the target environment, making the result closer to appearance harmonization than controllable relighting. To address this issue, we propose DynOLAT, a generalizable OLAT video prediction framework for dynamic full-body humans. Instead of directly synthesizing a single relit appearance, our method predicts temporally consistent One-Light-At-a-Time (OLAT) basis videos from flat-lit inputs, and then linearly combines the predicted bases according to the target environment map. This OLAT-based formulation makes the directional response explicit in the predicted bases, while the relative lighting strength is determined by the linear weights derived from the environment map. We further introduce a dynamic capture pipeline and the first large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT dataset, comprising over 24 million frames from 224 identity-outfit combinations, where different outfits of the same person define separate combinations. Experiments show that DynOLAT responds more faithfully to variations in target lighting direction and relative intensity than the tested baselines, enabling controllable video relighting while preserving fine appearance details and temporal coherence. The dataset and processing tools will be publicly released to foster future research.

title: Leakage-aware federated-style simulation for fraud risk prediction in AI-enabled FinTech platforms
abstract: AI-enabled FinTech platforms increasingly rely on automated fraud-risk prediction to secure high-volume digital payments, mobile-money transactions, and real-time financial services. However, fraud detection remains difficult because fraudulent transactions are rare, financial data are sensitive, and centralized machine-learning models may create privacy and data-governance risks. This study evaluates a leakage-aware and imbalance-aware federated-style simulation for fraud-risk prediction in AI-enabled FinTech platforms. The study does not implement FedAvg, cryptographic secure aggregation, differential privacy, or model-parameter exchange. Instead, the PaySim Synthetic Financial Dataset was partitioned into five simulated FinTech clients, local models were trained separately, and prediction-level aggregation was used to compare centralized and simulated decentralized learning settings. The experimental workflow included data-quality assessment, leakage-aware feature selection, feature engineering, class-imbalance analysis, centralized model development, threshold optimization, and federated-style model comparison. The results show that fraud cases represented only 0.0466% of all transactions and occurred only in CASH_OUT and TRANSFER operations. The best-balanced centralized model was the Improved Random Forest at a threshold of 0.33, achieving an F1-score of 0.3019. Federated Ensemble Aggregation achieved the highest PR-AUC of 0.2699 and a precision of 1.0000, but its recall remained low at 0.1429. The centralized Improved Random Forest retained the highest F1-score of 0.3019, indicating a stronger overall precision-recall balance. Global feature-importance analysis showed that transaction amount, log-transformed amount, temporal features, transaction type, and destination-account activity were the main fraud-risk indicators. These findings should be interpreted as evidence from simulated decentralized fraud-risk learning rather than a full secure federated learning implementation.

title: Viscot-steer: Disentangling and Transferring Visual Chain-of-Thought via Activation Steering
abstract: Visual chain-of-thought (visual-CoT), also known as "thinking with images", equips LVLMs with the ability to locate and use key visual evidence for reasoning. However, acquiring such visual-CoT capabilities requires costly post-training and tightly couples them to a specific backbone, making transfer to other LVLMs difficult. Existing cross-model transfer methods typically treat visual-CoT as a monolithic capability, using a unified representation that ignores the functional distinction between grounding and reasoning and introduces stage-irrelevant interventions. To address this problem, we propose Viscot-steer, a training-free activation steering framework for transferring visual-CoT capabilities across heterogeneous LVLMs. Specifically, Viscot-steer first disentangles visual-CoT into grounding and reasoning vectors and extracts them from the source-model layers associated with the corresponding capabilities. It then aligns the vectors with the activation space of the target model and steers the grounding and reasoning layers during bounding-box prediction and reasoning-trace generation, respectively. Across benchmarks covering high-resolution visual understanding, general visual perception and reasoning, and mathematical visual reasoning, Viscot-steer transfers capabilities from different visual-CoT models to architecturally diverse LVLMs and outperforms the strongest capability-transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 percentage points on the primary evaluation metrics.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Disguised Missing Values in Sensor Data — Code, Data and Results
abstract: Reproducibility artifacts for the ICDE 2027 Experiment, Analysis and Benchmark paper “Hidden in Plain Sight: Disguised Missing Values in Sensor Data and Their Silent Effects on Learned Models and Explanations”. Includes the DMV injection framework (4 placeholder types × 3 failure mechanisms), all detectors (including SENTRY and wrappers for the original FAHES and Raha), scripts for the 1,200-scenario benchmark, downstream XGBoost/SHAP study, real-DMV analysis and sensitivity study, the input datasets, raw result files for every table and figure, and a one-command reproduction script (run_all.sh)

title: Evidence-Grounded Iterative Reasoning for the Diagnosis of Diffuse Cystic Lung Diseases
abstract: Overlapping imaging manifestations complicate the differential diagnosis of Diffuse Cystic Lung Diseases (DCLDs), while limited annotated data constrain supervised model development. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can integrate imaging and clinical information, but their diagnostic reasoning remains limited by incomplete volumetric perception and insufficient grounding in disease-specific evidence. We propose DCLDs-EIR, an evidence-grounded iterative reasoning framework coupling diagnostic hypothesis refinement with multimodal evidence acquisition and verification. Multiview renderings of predicted lung and cyst segmentations characterize global cyst distributions and initialize the differential diagnosis. Competing hypotheses guide axial CT inspection to identify local findings that, together with clinical context, inform retrieval from a disease-specific knowledge graph. Accumulated patient observations and retrieved knowledge are jointly assessed for diagnostic support and refutation to revise the diagnostic state. Updated hypotheses and unresolved distinctions guide subsequent inspection, forming a feedback loop between evidence acquisition and hypothesis verification. Multicenter evaluation demonstrates that DCLDs-EIR consistently improves diagnostic accuracy over baselines and enables traceable differential diagnosis through explicit links between diagnostic hypotheses, patient observations, and disease-specific knowledge.

title: RealEmbedBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Application-Layer Embedded Software Tasks
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on general coding tasks, but their capabilities in application-layer embedded software development remain underexplored. Existing embedded benchmarks primarily focus on hardware-in-the-loop validation in simulated environments. We introduce RealEmbedBench, a benchmark of 5,142 samples covering three application-layer tasks: code generation and completion, state machine modeling and implementation, and cross-OS code translation. We evaluate six representative LLMs and find substantial performance differences across tasks and models. Project context, especially the local code window, significantly affects code generation and completion. Models perform reasonably well at state machine modeling but struggle to translate these models into executable code. Cross-OS translation performance varies substantially by direction. Translation from Harmony to RT-Thread is particularly challenging, with an average pass rate of 0.1667. These findings suggest that developers should consider local code context when using LLMs for code generation and completion and select models according to the translation direction. They also motivate the use of more real-world state machine implementation data in LLM training to narrow the gap between modeling and executable code.

title: PhysMoE: Fast Spatial Grounding with Single-Token Coordinate Representation in Modality-Decoupled VLMs
abstract: Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation. However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets. To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions: (1) sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference; (2) encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and (3) differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders. Compared to base models, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks. Our work is open-sourced at https://github.com/lrm20011/ps_moe_open.

title: MoT3DVG: A Benchmark for Outdoor 3D Visual Grounding with Motion-Aware Descriptions and Temporal Cues
abstract: 3D visual grounding (3DVG) localizes language-referred objects in 3D scenes, with broad applicability in both indoor and outdoor environments. However, existing 3DVG research focuses on static indoor objects, limiting its use in dynamic outdoor autonomous driving. Motion descriptions, which capture the temporal dynamics of moving objects, offer a promising way to address this challenge. We therefore introduce MoT3DVG, a large-scale dataset for dynamic-aware outdoor 3DVG with temporally evolving motion descriptions. It contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes dataset, and provides 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. We further propose DynaVG, a novel framework that effectively leverages temporal cues for outdoor 3DVG. In addition to the standard modality-specific encoders, DynaVG introduces a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding (SLIDE) module before the language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models both local motion cues and global temporal context via short-term window encoding and long-term window shifting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG, validating the effectiveness of motion-aware encoding. Our work reveals open challenges and promising directions for future research in outdoor 3DVG.

title: Not Yet in the Profile: Uncertainty-Aware Dynamic User Profiling by Learning from Future Interactions
abstract: On the Web, user profiling builds compact user representations from interaction histories for efficient personalization, and dynamic user profiling updates them as users' behavior and preferences change. However, new user behavior can be ambiguous, and its interpretation differs across users. To address this, we introduce Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Profile Manager (UAPM), which separates the claims in a user profile from interpretations of new behavior that are not yet confirmed, through a Profile, a Buffer, and a Rulebook. UAPM records user-specific interpretation and update rules in the Rulebook, keeps ambiguous evidence in the Buffer outside the Profile as evidence for later decisions, and writes supported general and situational characteristics to the Profile. We train UAPM with Privileged On-Policy Distillation with Dual Specialization (POPD-DS), which learns from recorded future interactions during training without access to them at deployment. Its first stage, Dual Specialization, distills a stronger model into a current-only Student and a future-informed model that becomes the Teacher. In the second stage, privileged on-policy distillation (POPD), only the fixed Teacher receives future interactions and guides the Student's own management decisions alongside task rewards. Experiments on three Web personalization tasks show that UAPM outperforms multiple baselines under the same downstream input budget, improving on the best same-budget baseline by up to 5%.

title: AKANE Architecture E2: Finding an LLM's mistakes from how its answers connect
abstract: Code, data, and results for small experiments in which a small language model (Gemma-2 2B) answers many true/false statements and writes its own consistency rules, some of them wrong. A network checks the model's answers against those rules while also doubting each rule, using belief propagation, and the signals are compared with the model's confidence and with counting rule violations.
